'''''Musa acuminata''''' is a species of [[banana]] native to [[South Asia|Southern Asia]], its range comprising the [[Indian subcontinent]] and [[Southeast Asia]]. Many of the modern edible dessert bananas are derived from this species, although some are hybrids with ''[[Musa balbisiana]]''.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20161210041528/http://aob.oxfordjournals.org/content/88/6/1017.short Genetic Diversity of the Wild Banana Musa acuminata Colla in Malaysia as Evidenced by AFLP], by Carol Wong, Ruth Kiew, Jin Phang Loh, Leong Huat Gan, Ohn Set, Sing Kong Lee, Shawn Lum and Yik Yuen Gan</ref> First cultivated by humans around 8000 BCE,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.buzzle.com/articles/history-of-bananas.html|title=History of Bananas|author=Chandramita Bora|work=Buzzle|access-date=2013-05-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160415042437/https://www.buzzle.com/articles/history-of-bananas.html|archive-date=2016-04-15|url-status=usurped}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.clas.ufl.edu/users/krigbaum/6930/mbida_etal_jas_2000.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=2013-05-09 |archive-date=2012-01-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120114191608/http://www.clas.ufl.edu/users/krigbaum/6930/mbida_etal_JAS_2000.pdf }}</ref> it is one of the early examples of [[List of domesticated plants|domesticated plants]].

[[File:Musa acuminata, Burdwan, West Bengal, India 29 09 2012.JPG|thumb|Fruit in [[West Bengal]], [[India]].]]

==Description==
''Musa acuminata'' is [[botanical terminology|classified by botanists]] as an [[herbaceous]] plant and an [[evergreen]] and a [[perennial]], but not as a [[tree]]. The trunk (known as the [[pseudostem]]) is made of tightly packed layers of [[leaf]] sheaths emerging from completely or partially buried [[corm]]s.<ref name="simmonds1962">{{cite journal|author=N.W. Simmonds|year=1962|title=Where our bananas come from|journal=New Scientist|volume=16|issue=307|pages=36–39|publisher=Reed Business Information|issn=0262-4079|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ooQ6YhL3rtMC&pg=PA36|access-date=2011-06-11 }}</ref> The leaves are at the top of the leaf sheaths, or [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] and in the subspecies M. a. truncata the blade or [[Lamina (leaf)|lamina]] is up to {{convert|22|ft|m}} in length and {{convert|39|in|m}} wide.

The [[inflorescence]] grows horizontally or obliquely from the trunk. The individual [[flower]]s are white to yellowish-white in color and are [[Geotropism|negatively geotropic]] (that is, growing upwards and away from the ground).<ref name="simmonds1962"/><ref name="hakkinen">{{cite journal|author1=Markku Häkkinen  |author2=Edmond De Langhe |name-list-style=amp |year=2001|title=''Musa acuminata'' in Northern Borneo|publisher=[[International Network for the Improvement of Banana and Plantain]]|url=http://bananas.bioversityinternational.org/files/files/pdf/publications/reportborneo.pdf|access-date=June 11, 2011 }}</ref> Both male and female flowers are present in a single inflorescence. Female flowers are located near the base (and develop into fruit), and the male flowers located at the tipmost top-shaped bud in between leathery [[bract]]s.<ref name="simmonds1962"/>

The rather slender fruits are [[berry (botany)|berries]], the size of each depends on the number of seeds they contain. Each fruit can have 15 to 62 seeds.<ref name="doijode">{{cite book|author=S. D. Doijode|title =Seed storage of horticultural crops|publisher =Routledge|year =2001|pages=69–71|isbn =978-1-56022-901-8|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=t8ggxMDbjTYC&pg=PA69}}</ref> Each fruit bunch can have an average of 161.76 ± 60.62 fingers with each finger around {{convert|2.4|by|9|cm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}} in size.<ref name="marod">{{cite journal|author1=Dokrak Marod |author2=Piya Pinyo |author3=Prateep Duengkae |author4=Tanaka Hiroshi  |name-list-style=amp |year=2010|title=The Role of Wild Banana (''Musa acuminata'' Colla) on Wildlife Diversity in Mixed Deciduous Forest, Kanchanaburi Province, Western Thailand|journal=Kasetsart Journal: Natural Science |volume=44|issue=1|pages=35–43|publisher=Kasetart University|url=http://kasetsartjournal.ku.ac.th/kuj_files/2010/A1001141018371250.pdf|access-date=2011-06-11 }}</ref>

The seeds of wild ''M. acuminata'' are around {{convert|5|to|6|mm|in|frac=32|abbr=on}} in diameter.<ref name="simmonds1962"/> They are subglobose or angular in shape and very hard. The tiny embryo is located at the end of the [[wikt:micropyle|micropyle]].<ref name="doijode"/> Each seed of ''M. acuminata'' typically produces around four times its size in edible starchy pulp (the [[parenchyma]], the portion of the bananas eaten), around {{convert|0.23|cm3|mm3 cuin|abbr=on}}.<ref name="simmonds1962"/><ref name="pillay"/> Wild ''M. acuminata'' is [[diploid]] with 2''n''=2''x''=22 [[chromosome]]s, while cultivated varieties ([[cultivar]]s) are mostly [[triploid]] (2''n''=3''x''=33) and [[Parthenocarpy|parthenocarpic]], meaning producing fruit without seeds. The most familiar dessert banana cultivars belong to the [[Cavendish bananas|Cavendish subgroup]]. These high yielding cultivars were produced through selection of the natural mutations resulting from the normal [[vegetative propagation]] of banana farming.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://publications.cirad.fr/une_notice.php?dk=544316|title=The genetic diversity of banana in figures|last=T.|first=Lescot|website=publications.cirad.fr|language=fr|access-date=2018-10-23}}</ref> The ratio of pulp to seeds increases dramatically in "[[Parthenocarpy|seedless]]" edible cultivars: the small and largely sterile seeds are now surrounded by 23 times their size in edible pulp.<ref name="pillay">{{cite book|author1=Michael Pillay  |author2=Abdou Tenkouano |name-list-style=amp |title =Banana Breeding and Production|publisher =CRC Press|year =2011|isbn =978-1-4398-0017-1|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=l191eUt9FSUC}}</ref> The seeds themselves are reduced to tiny black specks along the central axis of the fruit.<ref name="simmonds1962"/>

==Taxonomy==
''Musa acuminata'' belongs to [[Musa (genus)#Sections|section ''Musa'']] (formerly ''Eumusa'') of the genus ''Musa''. It belongs to the Family [[Musaceae]] of the Order [[Zingiberales]].<ref name=grin/> It is divided into several [[subspecies]] (see {{Slink||Subspecies}} section below).<ref name="ploetz"/>

''M. acuminata'' was first described by the Italian botanist [[Luigi Aloysius Colla]] in the book ''Memorie della Reale Accademia delle Scienze di Torino'' (1820).<ref name=powo/><ref name="karamura">{{cite book|author=Deborah A. Karamura|title =Numerical taxonomic studies of the East African Highland bananas (''Musa'' AAA-East Africa) in Uganda|publisher =Bioversity International|year =1999|page=18|isbn =978-2-910810-31-3|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=0coS_wuPjz4C&pg=PA18}}</ref> Although other authorities have published various names for this species and its hybrids mistaken for different species (notably ''Musa sapientum'' by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] which is now known to be a hybrid of ''M. acuminata'' and ''[[Musa balbisiana]]''), Colla's publication is the oldest name for the species and thus has precedence over the others from the rules of the [[International Code of Botanical Nomenclature]].<ref name="molina"/> Colla also was the first authority to recognize that both ''Musa acuminata'' and ''Musa balbisiana'' were wild ancestral species, even though the specimen he described was a naturally occurring seedless [[polyploid]] like cultivated [[banana]]s.<ref name="karamura"/>

The following are the most commonly accepted subspecies:<ref name="ploetz">{{cite journal|author1=Randy C. Ploetz |author2=Angela Kay Kepler |author3=Jeff Daniells |author4=Scot C. :Commonly known as [[blood banana]]s. Native to Java. It is cultivated as an ornamental plant for the dark red patches of color on their predominantly dark green leaves. In Hawaii it is known as the ''mai'a 'oa{{'}}'', and is of cultural and folk medicinal significance as the only seeded banana to be introduced to the islands before European contact.<ref name="ploetz"/>

==Distribution==
[[File:Musa acuminata ajith2(1).jpg|thumb|right|150px|Planting]]
''Musa acuminata'' is native to the [[Biogeography|biogeographical]] region of [[Malesia]] and most of mainland Indochina.<ref name="ploetz"/>

''M. acuminata'' favors wet tropical climates in contrast to the hardier ''[[Musa balbisiana|M. balbisiana]]'', the species it [[hybrid (biology)|hybrid]]ized extensively with to provide almost all modern cultivars of edible bananas.<ref name="kingsbury">{{cite book|author=Noël Kingsbury|title =Hybrid: the history and science of plant breeding|publisher=[[University of Chicago Press]] |year =2009|pages=31–32|isbn =978-0-226-43704-0|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=dGSj-CFxk-QC&pg=PA31}}</ref> Subsequent spread of the species outside of its native region is thought to be purely the result of human intervention.<ref name="daniells"/> Early farmers introduced ''M. acuminata'' into the native range of ''M. balbisiana'' resulting in hybridization and the development of modern edible clones.<ref name="elzebroek"/>

[[List of banana cultivars#AAB|AAB cultivars]] were spread from somewhere around the Philippines about 4 kya (2000 BCE) and resulted in the distinct banana cultivars known as the Maia Maoli or Popoulo group bananas in the Pacific islands. They may have been introduced as well to South America during [[Precolumbian]] times from contact with early [[Polynesian people|Polynesian]] sailors, although evidence of this is debatable.<ref name="daniells"/>

Westward spread included Africa which already had evidence of ''M. acuminata'' × ''M. balbisiana'' hybrid cultivation from as early as 1000 to 400 BCE.<ref name="daniells">{{cite book|author1=Jeffrey William Daniells  |author2=Suzanne L. Sharrock |name-list-style=amp |title =Musalogue, a catalogue of ''Musa'' germplasm: diversity in the genus ''Musa''|publisher =Bioversity International|year =2001|isbn =978-2-910810-42-9|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=lNBcPkUFGzkC}}</ref> They were probably introduced first to Madagascar from Indonesia.<ref name="elzebroek">{{cite book|author1=A. T. G. Elzebroek  |author2=Koop Wind |name-list-style=amp |title =Guide to cultivated plants|publisher =CABI|year =2001|pages=35–38|isbn =978-1-84593-356-2|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=YvU1XnUVxFQC&pg=PA35}}</ref>

From West Africa, they were introduced to the Canary islands by the Portuguese in the 16th century, and from there were introduced to Hispaniola (modern Haiti and the Dominican Republic) in 1516.<ref name="elzebroek"/>

==Ecology==
Wild ''Musa acuminata'' is propagated [[Sexual reproduction|sexually]] by seeds or [[Asexual reproduction|asexually]] by [[Sucker (botany)|sucker]]s. Edible [[Parthenocarpy|parthenocarpic]] cultivars are usually cultivated by suckers in plantations or [[cloning|cloned]] by [[tissue culture]].<ref name="ong"/> Seeds are also still used in research for developing new cultivars.<ref name="doijode"/>

''M. acuminata'' is a [[pioneer species]]. It rapidly exploits newly disturbed areas, like areas recently subjected to [[forest fire]]s. It is also considered a 'keystone species' in certain [[ecosystem]]s, paving the way for greater wildlife diversity once they have established themselves in an area. It is particularly important as a food source for wildlife due to its rapid regeneration.<ref name="marod"/>

''M. acuminata'' bears flowers that by their very structure, makes it difficult to self-pollinate. It takes about four months for the flowers to develop into fruits, with the fruit clusters at the bases ripening sooner than those at the tip.<ref name="marod"/>

A large variety of wildlife feeds on the fruits. These include [[Frugivore|frugivorous]] bats, birds, squirrels, tree shrews, civets, rats, mice, monkeys, and apes.<ref name="marod"/> These animals are also important for [[seed dispersal]].<ref name="tang">
:{{Cite journal|doi=10.1111/j.1744-7429.2009.00503.x|s2cid=83551835 |title=Seed Dispersal Distances and Plant Migration Potential in Tropical East Asia |date=2009 |last1=Corlett |first1=Richard T. |journal=Biotropica |volume=41 |issue=5 |pages=592–598 |bibcode=2009Biotr..41..592C }}
:
:This review cites this research.
:
:{{cite journal|author1=Zhanhui Tang|author2=Lianxi Sheng|author3=Xunfeng Ma|author4=Min Cao|author5=Stuart Parsons|author6=Jie Ma|author7=Shuyi Zhang|name-list-style=amp|year=2007|title=Temporal and spatial patterns of seed dispersal of ''Musa acuminata'' by ''Cynopterus sphinx''|journal=[[Acta Chiropterologica]]|volume=9|issue=1|pages=229–235|publisher=[[Museum and Institute of Zoology]], [[Polish Academy of Sciences]]|issn=1508-1109|url=http://www.eab.auckland.ac.nz/pdf/Tang%20et%20al%202007.pdf|access-date=2011-06-06|doi=10.3161/1733-5329(2007)9[229:taspos]2.0.co;2|s2cid=86011300 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180127072706/http://www.eab.auckland.ac.nz/pdf/Tang%20et%20al%202007.pdf|archive-date=2018-01-27}}
</ref>

Mature seeds germinate readily 2 to 3 weeks after sowing.<ref name="ong">{{cite book|author=Hean Chooi Ong|title =Vegetables for Health and Healing|publisher =Utusan Publications|year =2008|page=38|isbn =978-967-61-2102-8|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=COXOOzdNZ10C&pg=PA38}}</ref> Unsprouted, they can remain viable from a few months to two years of storage.<ref name="doijode"/> Nevertheless, studies show that [[Vegetative reproduction|clone]] plantlets are much more likely to survive than seedlings germinated from seeds.<ref name="marod"/>

==Domestication==
{{Main|Banana|Cooking banana}}
[[File:Green raw bananas.jpg|thumb|Green bananas not yet ripe]]
In 1955, Norman Simmonds and Ken Shepherd revised the classification of modern edible bananas based on their genetic origins. Their classification depends on how many of the characteristics of the two ancestral species (''Musa acuminata'' and ''Musa balbisiana'') are exhibited by the cultivars.<ref name="molina">{{cite book|author1=A.B. Molina  |author2=V.N. Roa |name-list-style=amp |title =Advancing Banana and Plantain R and D in Asia and the Pacific|publisher =International Network for the Improvement of Banana and Plantain – Asia and Pacific Network & the International Plant Genetic Resources Institute  |year =2000|page=57|isbn =978-971-91751-3-1|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=lV4k4j85r2AC&pg=PA57}}</ref> Most banana cultivars which exhibit purely or mostly ''Musa acuminata'' genomes are [[Banana|dessert bananas]], while hybrids of ''M. acuminata'' and ''M. balbisiana'' are mostly cooking bananas or [[Plantain (cooking)|plantain]]s.<ref name="valmayor">{{cite journal|author=R.V. Valmayor|year=2000|title=Cooking bananas – Classification, production and utilization in South-East Asia|journal=Infomusa|volume=9|issue=1|pages=28–30|publisher=International Network for the Improvement of Banana and Plantain|issn=1023-0076|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jPky4TEKB3YC&pg=PA28|access-date=2011-06-05}}</ref>

''Musa acuminata'' is one of the earliest plants to be [[List of domesticated plants|domesticated]] by humans for agriculture, 7,000 years ago in [[New Guinea]] and [[Wallacea]].<ref name="Purugganan-Fuller-2009">{{cite journal | last1=Purugganan | first1=Michael D. | last2=Fuller | first2=Dorian Q. | title=The nature of selection during plant domestication | journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | publisher=[[Nature Research]] | volume=457 | issue=7231 | year=2009 | issn=0028-0836 | doi=10.1038/nature07895 | pages=843–848| pmid=19212403 | bibcode=2009Natur.457..843P | s2cid=205216444 }}</ref> It has been suggested that ''M. acuminata'' may have originally been domesticated for parts other than the fruit. Either for fiber, for construction materials, or for its edible male bud.<ref name="sharrok">{{cite book|author1=Suzanne Sharrok  |author2=Emile Frison |name-list-style=amp |year=1998|chapter=Musa production around the world – trends, varieties and regional importance|title=Networking Banana and Plantain|issue=Annual Report|pages=42–47|publisher=International Network for the Improvement of Banana and Plantain & Bioversity International|access-date= July 23, 2011|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cuMH6LqHH-sC&pg=PA42}}</ref> They were selected early for [[parthenocarpy]] and seed [[Sterility (physiology)|sterility]] in their fruits, a process that might have taken thousands of years. This initially led to the first 'human-edible' banana diploid clones (modern [[List of banana cultivars#AA Group|AA cultivars]]). Diploid clones are still able to produce viable seeds when pollinated by wild species. This resulted in the development of [[triploid]] clones which were conserved for their larger fruit.<ref name="hather">{{cite book|chapter=Tracking the banana: its significance in early agriculture|author1=Edmond de Langhe  |author2=Pierre de Maret |name-list-style=amp |editor=Jon G. Hather|title =The Prehistory of Food: Appetites for Change|publisher =Routledge|year =2004|page=372|isbn =978-0-203-20338-5|chapter-url =https://books.google.com/books?id=DMgKW9HleFoC&pg=PA372}}</ref>

''M. acuminata'' was later introduced into mainland Indochina into the range of another ancestral wild banana species – ''[[Musa balbisiana]]'', a hardier species of lesser genetic diversity than ''M. acuminata''. Hybridization between the two resulted in drought-resistant edible cultivars. Modern edible banana and plantain cultivars are derived from permutations of hybridization and polyploidy of the two.<ref name="hather"/>

==Ornamental==
''M. acuminata'' is one of several banana species cultivated as an ornamental plant, for its striking shape and foliage. In [[temperateness|temperate]] regions it requires protection in winter, as it does not tolerate temperatures below {{convert| 10|C|F|abbr=on}}. The [[cultivar]] ''M. acuminata'' 'Dwarf Cavendish' (AAA Group) has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/56394/Musa-acuminata-Dwarf-Cavendish-(AAA-Group)-(F)/Details|title=Musa acuminata 'Dwarf Cavendish' (AAA Group) |website=Rhs.org.uk}}</ref><ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants – Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 65 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 2018-04-04}}</ref>
